item.title: The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
item.dc:creator: Matilde Catanese
item.description: This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

item.title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
item.dc:creator: Jee Young Lee; Sora Park; Janet Fulton
item.description: This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

item.title: Who fuels the fire? Predicting amplifiers, copycats, and attenuators in the networked spread of toxicity in immigration discourse
item.dc:creator: Yiqi Li; Aimei Yang
item.description: Drawing on Moral Foundations Theory and recent network diffusion studies, we examine the toxicity spread in US immigration-related discourse on X ( N = 305,878 tweets, January 2021 to April 2024). Using AI-assisted content analysis, this study examines how psychological predispositions (issue stance and moral foundations) and network positions predict users’ toxicity roles (i.e. amplifiers, copycats, and attenuators). Multinomial regression and random forest models reveal that amplifiers are typically centrally embedded users who score high on binding moral values, especially sanctity. Attenuators often hold pro-immigration stances and receive more inbound attention, suggesting reputational restraint and network moderation. Copycats, situated in dense, reciprocated ego networks, tend to reciprocate and mimic the tone of their peers. Contrary to expectations, amplification is not driven by bridge actors but by highly central users. This typology enhances our understanding of how moral convictions and network structures influence propagation, with implications for platform design and network intervention strategies.

item.title: Shadow archives in the age of extraction: Metadata, legitimacy, and the politics of Anna’s Archive
item.dc:creator: Ian Dunham
item.description: Anna’s Archive is a public index of illicit digital libraries that presents itself as a moral and technical infrastructure for global access to knowledge. Drawing on digital infrastructure ethnography, platform hermeneutics, and genealogical method, this article examines how the project negotiates legitimacy through metadata, discourse, and infrastructural design. I argue that Anna’s Archive transforms the logic of piracy into an infrastructure of visibility that mirrors and contests institutional archives, enacting a novel illicit politics of knowledge circulation. The study identifies four modes of legitimacy—pragmatic, moral, community, and cognitive—through which the archive sustains authority while remaining outside legal frameworks. By situating these practices within broader debates on platform accountability, data governance, and infrastructural justice, the article shows how shadow infrastructures expose the power relations and politics of access that underlie contemporary regimes of information extraction.

item.title: Brand governance in the platform economy: From political to regulatory recognition
item.dc:creator: Marco Scalvini
item.description: This article reconceptualises corporate advocacy as brand governance, a techno-normative promotional practice that regulates the conditions of political visibility within networked publics. Drawing on a sociosemiotic analysis of global advocacy campaigns (2017–2022), the analysis identifies three strategies, Visionary (“Feeling the Other”), Sensitive (“Feeling for Others”) and Reflexive (“Feeling with Others”), each operating through distinct affective and narrative logics. The argument advances a distinction between political and regulatory recognition. Political recognition acknowledges claims in their structural and collective dimension; regulatory recognition extends legitimacy only to claims aligned with the promotional regime’s affective and reputational logic. The evidence suggests that brand governance operates predominantly in this regulatory mode, producing a conditional visibility that privileges individualised emotional appeals over structural political demands. This study focuses on US and Western European promotional cultures; comparative research across other regions remains a necessary next step.

item.title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
item.dc:creator: Atle Haugsgjerd; Rune Karlsen; Tine Figenschou; Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk; Toril Aalberg
item.description: A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

item.title: Overconfident youth, underconfident elders: Age differences in algorithmic knowledge confidence and information perceptions
item.dc:creator: Myojung Chung
item.description: Age-related differences in algorithmic knowledge are typically interpreted as competence gaps that render younger “digital natives” better equipped and older users more vulnerable in algorithmically curated environments. This study challenges these assumptions by examining (a) algorithmic knowledge confidence—whether users’ subjective algorithmic knowledge exceeds or falls short of their algorithmic awareness and knowledge—and (b) what consequences such misalignment has for information environment perceptions. Using US survey data ( N = 1205), this study found systematic misalignment between subjective and awareness-based algorithmic knowledge: younger users overestimate their understanding, whereas older users underestimate theirs. Social media use partially mediated the age–knowledge confidence relationship. Knowledge confidence, in turn, predicted perceived information reliability and diversity. These findings reveal that critical assessment of information environment is determined not by knowledge level alone but by alignment between subjective and awareness-based knowledge, highlighting the need for age-tailored interventions addressing knowledge overconfidence and underconfidence.
